answers.answer: Fifty boxes of earth were shipped from Varna to Whitby and delivered to the old chapel at Carfax. Twenty-one were later removed (nine taken from a Piccadilly house, six each to Bermondsey and Mile End). Twenty-nine stayed at Carfax; on 3 October the party found eight boxes in the Carfax dining-room, and the text says one box was still unaccounted for. The passages do not fully reconcile the count of boxes found at Carfax.
First mention is in Mina Murray's journal, 26 July 1893: Lucy 'has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep', and Mrs Westenra had raised it with Mina, who locked their door at night.

Only Lucy's diary entry of 12 September 1893 (the 'Good-night, everybody' entry with the garlic and Ophelia lines) never mentions Arthur. The other eight of her nine documents (her May letters to Mina, the 19 August letter, the 23, 25 August and 9, 17 September diary entries, and the 17 September memorandum) all name Arthur.

Four transfusions, in order: (1) Arthur Holmwood, 7 September; (2) Dr Jack Seward, 10 September; (3) Van Helsing, 13 September (he rolled up his sleeve and Seward was told to operate); (4) Quincey Morris, 18 September. Quincey's line 'the blood of four strong men' confirms the count of four.

The garlic came from Haarlem, from Vanderpool's glass-houses, arriving as a big parcel from abroad (later a boxful every day). Van Helsing arranged them himself: he placed the flowers in Lucy's room, rubbed them round the windows and door, and made the wreath she wore.
First appearance is in Jonathan Harker's journal, 5 May 1893, at Bistritz, where he glosses the Slovak and Servian words 'vrolok' and 'vlkoslak' as 'were-wolf or vampire'.

One letter in his own hand: Quincey P. Morris to Arthur Holmwood, 25 May 1893, inviting Arthur to a camp-fire evening with Jack Seward, signed 'Yours, as ever and always, QUINCEY P. MORRIS'. Everything else about him is reported by others (for example Seward's note that 'Quincey wrote me a line too').

experience: The task log started empty each time, which made a clean start easy. Grep was the most useful tool: its per-passage snippets, entry IDs and per-entry counts let me see at a glance which documents were involved, and the 'more not shown (raise --limit)' line told me where more hits lay. The output is also long, which made it hard to scan. The search output mixed relevant passages with noise; for 'boxes of earth' the top hit was a 'part 18/19' passage about the sterilising of Carfax, not the count, and the Quincey search returned passages about other people. The semantic exception warnings ('This passage is one part of a longer record... `around ID`' and 'Cut off mid-thought') were accurate but added a read step to nearly every hit. Two things got in the way. My `list --by-entry --grep` call was refused because that flag does not exist; the help text says grep takes a positional phrase, and I should have had that spelled out in the usage line. The `--source Morris` filter matched only one passage, because most of Quincey's voice reaches the record through Seward's and Mina's diaries, not as his own narration. I wished the tool said which narrator's own writing a passage is, and whether a filter matched by narrator or by document, so that 'in his own hand' could be answered directly. The 'part N/M' tags were helpful for judging whether a passage was cut short.
